ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a relaxed, collegial videoconference style with mostly short-to-medium turns, though formal presentations are long and uninterrupted. The opening contains frequent overlap, greetings, tech checks, casual side chat, and clipped, sometimes fragmented speech; speakers use fillers such as “um,” “yeah,” “okay,” “right,” and repeated words or self-corrections. Formality shifts noticeably: introductions and talks are structured and professional but still conversational, while Q&A is informal, supportive, and exploratory. Questions are often prefaced with praise or hedging (“great talk,” “I have a naive question,” “I’m just curious”), then develop through follow-ups and reformulations. Participants generally build on prior remarks rather than sharply challenge them, expressing uncertainty openly with phrases like “I think,” “maybe,” “we don’t know,” and “it could be.” Disagreement or correction is indirect and softened, usually framed as an alternative interpretation or limitation. Responses tend to be generous and explanatory, with speakers acknowledging good questions, conceding gaps, and thinking aloud.

Meeting style for this meeting (quick_checkin): A rushed weekly check-in. People give short status updates and ask each other quick questions. Most turns are one or two sentences. Nobody summarizes. Someone has another meeting soon and the conversation stops where it stops.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Okay, so, quick one from me- the export finished last night, mostly.
  - Mostly?
  - Two of the sites didn't come through. I haven't looked yet.
Opening: Start with someone saying what they most want out of this meeting, briefly and casually.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Working out why wild bee numbers on farms did not recover after wildflower strips were planted along field edges.

speakers.name: Dr. Aisha Rahman
speakers.background: Landscape ecologist with 12 years of experience designing and evaluating agri-environment monitoring projects in intensively farmed lowland landscapes. She has built GIS-based connectivity models, conducted field assessments of floral and nesting resources, and coordinated repeated pollinator surveys across farm networks. On this programme, she has helped standardise strip-condition records and link farm locations to surrounding land-cover data.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Aisha treats the strips as components of a landscape rather than isolated interventions. She will argue that successful floral establishment does not establish whether strips provide bare ground, tussocky vegetation, hedgerows, banks, or other nesting substrates, nor whether they are reachable from source populations. She is especially alert to scale mismatch: a strip can look good at field-edge scale while remaining too isolated, too short-lived, or embedded in a hostile matrix to change farm-level bee populations.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Tomás Velasco
speakers.background: Bee biologist with 9 years of experience in wild-bee taxonomy, trait-based community analysis, and pesticide-risk research. His work combines specimen identification, pollen and foraging observations, reproductive-condition assays, and controlled exposure studies, with recent collaborations on linking field pesticide residues to sublethal effects in solitary bees and bumblebees. He manages the survey-specimen workflow for the county programme but is cautious about inferring individual-level mechanisms from the existing abundance data.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Tomás focuses on which bees were measured, not only how many. He expects a pooled abundance or richness result to conceal divergent responses among short-range solitary bees, long-range bumblebees, dietary specialists, and species with different nesting requirements. He will raise the possibility that pesticides or nutritional limitations reduce fecundity, larval development, navigation, or overwinter survival without causing conspicuous acute mortality. He will press the group to ask whether the current June and August surveys can detect demographic responses, colonisation lags, or species turnover.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

speakers.name: Dr. Eleanor Price
speakers.background: Agricultural economist in her third postdoctoral year, studying farmer participation in environmental schemes using payment records, cost surveys, interviews, and econometric analysis of land-use and crop-return decisions. She has worked with arable farmers on establishment costs, maintenance burdens, perceived yield effects near field margins, and how contract rules shape management choices. She is currently linking the programme's payment and management records to farm-level crop and field-size information.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Eleanor views strip quality and persistence as outcomes partly produced by incentives, risk, and farm constraints. She will ask whether uniform or area-based payments reward visible hectares more reliably than seed-mix quality, timely maintenance, reduced chemical exposure, or placement in ecologically connected locations. She will distinguish biological non-response from uneven implementation driven by opportunity costs, labour, machinery access, expected crop losses, and the distribution of semi-natural habitat across participating farms. She is interested in redesigns that are credible to farmers while making ecological performance measurable rather than assumed.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

benchmark_task: Give an interdisciplinary meeting with a main research question. The evaluated AI must propose relevant follow-up questions integrating the disciplines; novelty, usefulness and feasibility require expert judgment.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give an interdisciplinary meeting with a main research question. The evaluated AI must propose relevant follow-up questions integrating the disciplines; novelty, usefulness and feasibility require expert judgment.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Run a planning meeting involving one ecologist, one bee biologist and one agricultural economist. They should agree on the main research question: why have wild bee populations not recovered following field-edge wildflower-strip planting, and how should the intervention and incentive scheme be redesigned? Each participant should briefly explain the evidence and constraints their field considers relevant. The ecologist should note that flower strips may not supply nesting resources or connect suitable habitat at the relevant landscape scale. The biologist should note that responses may differ by species and foraging range, and that pesticide exposure could impair reproduction or survival without producing obvious mortality. The economist should note that farmers face varying establishment and upkeep costs, possible yield trade-offs, and subsidy incentives that may favour visible strip area rather than ecological performance. The discussion should leave the relative importance of these mechanisms unresolved and identify that linked ecological, biological and economic follow-up questions are needed. Do not have participants generate a final ranked list of follow-up questions or solve the research problem.

ground_truth.main_research_question: Why did wild bee abundance and species richness fail to recover after wildflower strips were planted, and what ecologically effective and economically workable redesign of strips and farm incentives could produce recovery?

relevant_integrated_follow_up_questions.question: Do bee responses depend on whether strips are connected to nesting habitat and other semi-natural patches within the foraging ranges of particular bee species, rather than on strip area alone?
relevant_integrated_follow_up_questions.integration: Combines landscape connectivity and nesting resources with species-specific foraging biology; it can identify where spatial targeting of payments is more effective than uniform field-edge planting.
relevant_integrated_follow_up_questions.feasibility: Map habitat and nesting proxies around surveyed farms, identify focal bee taxa, and relate multi-year occupancy or abundance changes to connectivity at several biologically informed spatial scales.

relevant_integrated_follow_up_questions.question: Are pesticide exposure and nutritional conditions jointly reducing bee reproduction or survival, so that flower availability in strips is insufficient to produce population growth?
relevant_integrated_follow_up_questions.integration: Links strip floral resources and farm management to bee physiology and sublethal pesticide effects, while considering whether management changes require compensation or altered subsidy conditions.
relevant_integrated_follow_up_questions.feasibility: Pair pesticide-use records and targeted residue sampling with floral-resource measurements and a focused set of biomarkers or reproduction/survival indicators for common focal species.

relevant_integrated_follow_up_questions.question: Which strip designs and maintenance schedules provide season-long forage and nesting opportunities while remaining acceptable to farmers given costs, labour, crop-yield risk and payments?
relevant_integrated_follow_up_questions.integration: Connects ecological resource requirements and bee phenology with establishment and maintenance costs, yield effects and incentive design.
relevant_integrated_follow_up_questions.feasibility: Compare existing seed mixes and mowing or re-sowing practices, measure flowering continuity and nesting features, and use farm budget data plus stated-preference or contract-choice analysis.

relevant_integrated_follow_up_questions.question: Would outcome-oriented or spatially targeted subsidies increase adoption of the strip locations and management practices most likely to benefit bees, compared with payments based mainly on planted area?
relevant_integrated_follow_up_questions.integration: Uses ecological and biological indicators to define credible outcomes or targeting rules, then assesses farmer participation, payment levels and administrative feasibility.
relevant_integrated_follow_up_questions.feasibility: Model alternative payment rules using observed farm costs and landscape data; test farmer willingness and monitoring burden through a small pilot before programme-wide implementation.

relevant_integrated_follow_up_questions.question: Are apparent null effects masking gains in some bee groups and losses in others, and do those differences correspond to landscape setting, pesticide exposure and farm-management incentives?
relevant_integrated_follow_up_questions.integration: Combines improved species identification and trait-based biology with ecological heterogeneity and economically driven management variation.
relevant_integrated_follow_up_questions.feasibility: Reanalyse repeated survey data by species or functional group, supplement identification where needed, and link responses to farm-level management and landscape covariates.

key_evidence_needed: Repeated, species-resolved bee data across more than two years, including measures related to reproduction or persistence where feasible.
Spatial data on floral resources, nesting-resource proxies and connectivity to semi-natural habitat at multiple foraging-relevant distances.
Farm-level pesticide applications or credible exposure proxies, plus targeted residue and sublethal-effect measurements.
Records of strip seed mix, planting, mowing, reseeding and other maintenance actions.
Farm-specific establishment, maintenance and opportunity costs, crop-yield effects, subsidy payments and farmer preferences for alternative contracts.
important_dependencies: Species and trait identification is needed before selecting meaningful spatial scales and focal taxa.
Access to confidential pesticide and economic records requires farmer consent and data-governance arrangements.
Any outcome-based payment pilot depends on selecting indicators that are ecologically meaningful, sufficiently reliable and not excessively costly to monitor.
Causal conclusions require comparison across landscape contexts and management regimes, and ideally matched comparison farms or staggered changes in implementation.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Morning, everyone. I’m hoping today we can get a bit clearer on whether this is a strip problem or a landscape problem, or more likely, where the two overlap.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: I'd add that a strip can look established, but the costly bits vary a lot from farm to farm. Timely upkeep, spray buffers, where it sits relative to productive crop. I'm seeing similar enrolled areas but very different maintenance entries in the records. I need to check whether that's real or just reporting. Aisha, which connectivity measures could we actually use in a payment scheme without surveying every field from scratch?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: I’d probably use a small set of map-based indicators, not a bespoke model. Things like the amount of semi-natural habitat and hedgerow connectivity within species-relevant distances, and whether the strip actually links to a patch. But broad maps will miss banks and little fallow corners, so I think we’d still need a quick field check on a subset. And Eleanor, are the more connected edges usually the ones farmers can’t afford to take out of production?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Tomás Velasco
transcript.text: Mm, species-relevant distances, yes.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: That’s exactly what I need to find out. I don’t think it’ll be uniform. On larger, more productive fields, the connected edge may have a pretty visible crop-return cost, but I need to link the strip locations to the crop and field-size data before I can say that. If we can identify those cases, a flat per-hectare payment may be selecting the cheaper edges instead of the most useful ones.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Right, that could matter.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Tomás Velasco
transcript.text: And the biological payoff could differ even along the same edge. Aisha, do those map layers tell us anything about actual nesting, um, substrate, or just nearby green cover? Because a strip can look well connected on paper and still be useless to, say, the small ground-nesting solitary bees that seem to be staying scarce.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Mostly nearby green cover, honestly. The maps can give us hedges and larger semi-natural patches, but not exposed soil, old banks, tussock structure, or those tiny neglected corners. So for nesting we'd need field checks, or rather at least a stratified subset of farms.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Tomás Velasco
transcript.text: That’s probably essential. I’m a little wary of treating nesting as a generic covariate. Bare ground helps some taxa and harms others, so could the field check- could it record a few discrete features rather than just score "nesting quality"? And I need to see whether the stored material is good enough to make those small solitary-bee identifications reliable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Discrete features makes more sense. We could record exposed ground, south-facing banks, tussocky grass, hedge bases, maybe cavities in dead wood, separately, and then not pretend one score fits every bee. If your IDs give us the main nesting guilds, we can stratify the visits around those rather than trying to inspect all- rather than trying to inspect all 24 the same way.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Tomás Velasco
transcript.text: That helps. One thing I don't want us to lose is that June and August are only two snapshots. If the strips are filling a mid-season gap, or if recruitment is failing over winter, those counts may barely, barely show it. The 2025 batches give me a tentative bumblebee-versus-small-solitary split, but I need to check the IDs and the sampling consistency before we build around that.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: And with only the 24 farms, I’d be careful about reading a June to August average as the strip effect anyway. Those two dense-looking strips with flat June counts, compared with that less impressive 2025 site, might be a phenology or species-composition, um, difference. Once you’ve checked the IDs, could we see whether those contrasts are actually bumblebees versus solitary bees?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Tomás Velasco
transcript.text: I think so, as long as the specimens are retained well enough. I can audit the 2025 material against the field sheets before we call those patterns biological. But I'd also want to compare within season rather than average it. If the bumblebees are using late flowers and the solitary taxa- if they need nesting access or earlier forage, the same strip could look both successful and unsuccessful.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Mm, that distinction matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: That makes me think the redesign can't just pay for a flowered hectare if different taxa need different things at different points. Tomás, once you've got the ID split, are there a couple of indicators, like early forage or a specific nesting feature, that actually mean something but are simple enough for a farmer or adviser to record without turning this into a huge compliance exercise?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Tomás Velasco
transcript.text: Probably, but I'd keep it really taxon-specific. An adviser could note early-flowering continuity, patches of exposed soil or a south-facing bank, and whether spraying is kept away from the strip. The trouble is, a cavity-nester and a ground-nester shouldn't get the same- shouldn't be using the same checklist. We may end up with two or three focal guilds, if the specimens support it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Two or three focal guilds would also stop us forcing one landscape scale onto everything. Since these are only 24 arable farms and the strips went in spring 2023, I’d use the next visits to contrast, say, isolated versus connected sites within each guild, rather than- rather than chasing a single overall bee response.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: And that gives us something we could potentially contract around without pretending every farm needs the same strip. The question for me is whether connected sites also systematically cost more in foregone crop or awkward machinery turns. If they do, we need to know whether a connectivity supplement would actually move, move placement, rather than just pay farms already able to provide it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Tomás Velasco
transcript.text: Hm, placement versus uptake.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Exactly. From the landscape side, I’d want to separate farms where a connected edge was genuinely available from ones where the whole surrounding matrix is, I mean, pretty isolated. Otherwise, a supplement could look ineffective just because there was nowhere useful to put the strip.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: That availability constraint matters for the payment analysis too. We should probably distinguish a farm that chooses a cheap isolated edge from one that just has no connected option. Otherwise we'll call it poor implementation when it's really a landscape- when it's really a landscape feasibility problem. Do you think the maps can flag that before we go out, even roughly?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Roughly, yes. I can map semi-natural cover, hedge networks, strip-to-patch distance, and identify farms with no plausible connected edge at a couple of candidate scales; I’d want Tomás’s trait groups before fixing those scales. But I wouldn’t use that as the final answer on nesting features—the maps are a triage tool, then we field-check the contrasting cases.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: That triage would be really useful. Then I can compare payment and maintenance patterns among farms with a plausible connected option, instead of treating all 24 as if they faced the same choice. I’ll need to check what location detail and permissions we actually have in the payment files, though. At the moment, I’m not sure the confidential records are clean enough to compare at the edge level.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Oh, that’s a constraint.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Tomás Velasco
transcript.text: And separately, Eleanor, what could farmers realistically tell us about spray timing and products near the strips? I’m not saying residues are the explanation from these counts, far from it. But a flower-rich edge can still be an exposure route, and the sublethal, sublethal stuff won’t show up as dead bees in a survey.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: I don't know yet, honestly. The management records may have broad declarations, but timing and products near a particular strip are unlikely to be reliable enough on their own. Farmer interviews or spray diaries would be much better, and I need to check whether there's budget and consent for that. We could at least ask about the decision points, whether they can leave a buffer and what makes that difficult in a given- in a particular season.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Tomás Velasco
transcript.text: I’d rather not make residue sampling the first ask if it makes people defensive. A small voluntary diary, diary with product class, timing, and whether the strip or its flowering period was adjacent to an application, might at least tell us whether targeted pollen or nectar samples are worth doing on a few contrasting farms. Does that seem feasible, or is even that too much reporting?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: I think a voluntary, very short diary is probably workable if we frame it as learning about constraints, not checking compliance. But I'd want to test that with a few farmers first. During spraying windows, even a simple extra form may be one more thing that drops off. If we do it, linking it to the mapped contrasting sites would make the burden a bit more defensible.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: I think that’s the sensible overlap. Map the contrasts first, then only ask for diaries and nesting checks where they can actually help distinguish explanations. I’m still waiting on the trait split before I settle the buffers, but I can start with the land-cover— I can start with the land-cover triage now.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Tomás Velasco
transcript.text: Yeah, selective sampling then.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: I’ll check whether we can get the edge-level payment and crop-return linkage cleared, and whether there’s even a small budget for piloting the diary with a few of those contrasting farms. If that access falls through, we should be honest that we can describe implementation differences, but not really identify the incentive, the incentive mechanism.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Yep, that sounds right.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Tomás Velasco
transcript.text: Okay, I think we should let people go a few minutes early. I’ll check the 2025 material, and we can pick this up once the map triage and, um, access questions are a bit clearer. Thanks, both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: Thanks, both—speak soon.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Cheers, bye.
